#6657. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

#6656. The Fall Winter 2026 Shoe Trends to Shop Now—From Kitten Heels to Great Boots

Fall’s top shoe trends pick up where we left off in the spring—iterating on classic shapes while infusing them with personality-driven touches. The result? Styles that feel both familiar and new; wearable yet a touch unexpected. And with the spring/summer 2027 collections now unfolding in real time, it’s clear that many of fall’s biggest trends are here to stay.

The kitten heel was a reference point for many designers—Celine, Prada, and Proenza Schouler included—who reworked pared-back silhouettes with playful, feminine flourishes. We’ve seen plenty already on the streets of New York Fashion Week. (Those looking for a little more height can turn to options from Victoria Beckham, Jil Sander, and Stella McCartney.)

Elsewhere, designers reimagined the T-strap—in both heeled sandal and pump form. It’s a perfect transitional shoe—sturdier than a flip-flop, but still perfectly suitable for a warm day. Though, for the colder months, you can pair it with knee-high or crew socks the way Dries Van Noten and Fendi did. Speaking of the colder months, boot season is upon us, and the runways displayed a handful of key silhouettes in that space, including the stretchy sock boot in both knee-high and ankle-height iterations, as well as rugged biker boots.

Slippers made their mark for fall too—from the return of classics like Gucci’s fur-lined horse-bit style to patterned and embroidered takes from Ralph Lauren and Conner Ives. A slip-on brings an ease to daily dressing, adding a polished feel to worn-in jeans and a laid-back cool to skirts. Plus, it’s a welcome flat alternative for party dressing and winter occasions. If heels are more your speed, you’ll find lovely festive options, from Chanel’s two-tone metallic glove pumps to Michael Kors’ red satin square-toed heels—like ornaments for the feet!

Already spotted on the spring summer 2027 runways in New York, kitten heels, textured pumps, and slip-on silhouettes are set to continue their reign. Now is the time to invest in styles that will carry you through the winter and into spring. Below, a closer look at all the top fall/winter 2026 shoe trends.

Don’t miss the rest of our fall/winter 2026 fashion coverage, from the fall fashion trends to know to the handbag styles that complement these looks best.

Biker boots are back in the driver's seat for fall, bringing a rugged, rebellious spirit to even the most feminine looks. At Balenciaga, slouchy black leather boots had a deliberately worn-in attitude, while Dries Van Noten and Proenza Schouler played with the contrast between sturdy footwear and softer, more romantic clothes. For a similar effect, try Balenciaga's buckled motor boots or Dries Van Noten's oxblood leather styles, while Dior's more polished riding-inspired boots offer a sleeker alternative. Frye's classic harness boots and distressed brown suede styles with spurs bring a little Western flair into the mix. Whether you prefer a tall, slouchy silhouette or something shorter and more rugged, these boots are particularly good at toughening up a feminine skirt or dress.

Sleek, streamlined, and endlessly flattering, the sock boot offers a more refined alternative to fall's rugged footwear. At Chanel, pastel-colored boots brought an unexpected softness to eveningwear, while Celine's pointed-toe iterations lent a ladylike finish to romantic skirts. Calvin Klein and Altuzarra favored a more minimalist approach, with supple leather boots that hugged the leg. Celine's glossy black stilettos and Reformation's buttery cream ankle boots capture the silhouette's elegant appeal, while Toteme's burgundy knee-highs introduce a welcome touch of color. For something more understated, Vince's slender black boots and Staud's low-heeled leather ankle style are equally compelling. Whether worn with a midiskirt or tucked beneath tailored trousers, the appeal lies in the silhouette's clean, uninterrupted line.

'Tis the season to put your best foot forward! With holiday invitations piling up, there's no better excuse to indulge in a little festive footwear. On the fall runways, Carolina Herrera and Michael Kors embraced old-Hollywood glamour with elegant evening pumps, while Tory Burch and Ferragamo made a case for shoes with a little extra shine. And why stop at a little? Chanel's crinkled gold leather pumps, Aeyde's silver metallic heels, and Ferragamo's sculptural gold mules are practically made for the dance floor. For a pop of festive red, look to Michael Kors's satin pumps or Aeyde's sleek mules, while Tory Burch's embellished Mary Janes and Herbert Levine's satin heels bring a little whimsy to the occasion. Whether you're dressing for a black-tie affair or cocktails with friends, consider these your invitation to have a little fun from the ankles down.

Fall’s kitten heel marries uptown elegance with downtown edge, thanks to unexpected touches like intricate embellishments and modern hardware. For the on-the-go woman, it’s a sensible style for the 9-to-9—with plenty of personality, to boot.

The slipper’s (or soft loafer, in some instances) effortless yet trend-forward nature was illustrated at Conner Ives and Calvin Klein, where it grounded statement skirts and sequined dresses, respectively. A hybrid of the ballet flat and mule, we love it styled with baggy, wide-leg jeans and a military jacket for an eclectic twist.

The fall/winter 2026 runways went wild for animal print. Leopard, snakeskin, zebra, and even abstract iterations appeared across footwear styles. For the minimalist, take a cue from Khaite and pair snakeskin pumps with rinse-wash denim. Or, for a more maximalist take, look to Isabel Marant, where crimson jeans proved the ideal complement to zebra-print tall boots.

Playing with shape also meant designers revisited the heel itself. The result? Cone heels made their way en masse onto the fall/winter 2026 runways. As seen on pumps, slingbacks, and leather and suede boots, the sculptural silhouette instantly sharpens your look. For right now, reach for a rounded-toe style that slips effortlessly beneath tailored trousers and straight-leg jeans.

A favorite in recent seasons, the fashion pump continues to reign supreme. For fall 2026, fresh takes walked the runway at Stella McCartney, Chanel, and Tory Burch—from barely there glove pumps to pop of color slingbacks. We love it rendered in unexpected hues and playful prints for right now.

The wild card crowdpleaser? Statement shoes! Whether in heeled or flat form, these whimsical creations balance summer’s playful energy with fall’s gravitas. Reach for textured pumps or sequined sneakers to add an unexpected pop to any look. No matter the occasion or destination, they bring a little fancy footwork to every step.

The T-strap makes its return for fall! Dior and Givenchy presented open-toe styles that can easily be added to your transitional rotation. Come later in the season, lean into the trend with a sharp pointed toe and a sock styled underneath. The shape is a natural match for an elegant midiskirt, as seen at Calvin Klein, Dries Van Noten, and Fendi.

#6652. We Tried Starbucks’ All-New Holiday Drinks—Here’s What We’d Order Again

I don’t care whether your annual traditions call for the start of the Christmas season on November 1 or you’re a total Scrooge until after Thanksgiving, Starbucks’ holiday menu is officially here—which means it’s time to retire the Pumpkin Spice Lattes (for now) and embrace your holly-er, jollier alter ego.

Naturally, I had to get my hands on the new flavors—and reacquaint myself with the classics—in the name of journalism and the holiday spirit! From the dessert-inspired tiramisu drinks to the light and bright Refreshers (there are two, by the way!), I put Starbucks’ latest creations to the test. Here’s which ones I’d order again—and what I’d skip.

If you want your coffee to taste like a straight-up dessert, good news: I found the morning pick-me-up for you. Starbucks has created the ultimate holiday treat in this Tiramisu Velvet Latte. Inspired by the classic Italian treat, the new signature drink combines espresso, milk, and vanilla syrup with a fluffy Velvet Mascarpone Cold Foam and cocoa dusting that mimics the OG. It’s sweet without being overly sweet, and the cold foam adds a rich, creamy layer like the actual dessert. Whether you get it hot or iced, it’s a fun departure from your typical Peppermint Mocha order.

Cold brew purists, this one’s for you. Starbucks is also giving its classic Cold Brew a holiday makeover with the same formula as its latte: vanilla syrup, Velvet Mascarpone Cold Foam, and a dusting of cocoa and coffee. Unlike the latte, this format allows the coffee to do more of the talking, and the creamy mascarpone foam adds just a touch of dessert energy.

Now, there are actually two ways to try the refresher: the classic version, a.k.a. the Apple Pomegranate Refresher, with crisp apple flavors and popping pomegranate-flavored pearls; and the Snowy Apple Drink, which features the same ingredients with coconut milk for a creamier take.

The classic refresher is definitely brighter and fruitier, with a tart-sweet apple flavor and sugary pops of pomegranate, while the Snowy Apple Drink is more mellowed out thanks to the coconut milk. The result still captures the key flavors, but delivers them with a smoother, creamier finish.

You can customize the refreshers even more by adding a citrusy twist of lemonade or adjusting the caffeine levels—anywhere from no caffeine to light caffeine to full-blown Energy Refresher.

While I genuinely enjoyed trying all three new beverages, I probably wouldn’t order the Tiramisu Velvet Latte again—but that’s only because the Tiramisu Velvet Cold Brew exists. I’m always going to gravitate toward a more coffee-forward drink. And as for the Apple Pomegranate Refreshers, they’re a fun addition to the lineup—light, fruity, and the perfect pick-me-up for after a long day of Christmas shopping (especially if you add the caffeine boost).

#6651. Failproof Homestyle Chicken Kari

This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

#6649. Blanca Miró and Larkspur & Hawk Celebrate Their Colorful Jewelry Collaboration With a Cocktail Party

"I wanted to let the jewelry shine, so I decided to wear something minimal," Blanca Miró told Vogue on Wednesday evening. Minimal, of course, is a relative term. The Barcelona-based designer, known for her exuberant approach to color and pattern, was dressed in head-to-toe orange, accessorized with vintage woven Prada pumps (which she owns in several colorways).

The occasion was a cocktail party celebrating her new collaboration with Larkspur & Hawk, the New York jewelry label founded by Emily Satloff. The two designers, along with their third co-host, writer and tastemaker Tatiana Hambro Arader, gathered friends at Thirty8East, a private art gallery founded by Ashlee Harrison and housed in an Upper East Side townhouse, where an exhibition titled Origins is currently on showcase. On the agenda: a collection of candy-colored rivière necklaces, bracelets, rings, and earrings that marries Miró's playful sensibility with Satloff's fascination with Georgian-era jewelry.

The collection could be spotted around the necks, dangling from the ears, and sparkling on the fingers of guests throughout the room. All three hosts wore the same colorful rivière necklace, though each styled it differently. Satloff paired hers with a vintage floral-jacquard skirt and black high-necked top, while Hambro Arader wore hers backwards, cascading down the open back of a lavender Colleen Allen dress. Three women, one necklace, and three entirely different approaches to getting dressed. Elsewhere, guests including Maria de la Orden, Batsheva Hay, Angelica Hicks, Charlotte Groeneveld, Becky Malinsky Shiah, and Lilly Sisto mingled over Champagne.

The collection features vibrant hues of red, blue, green, and yellow, including a playful take on stripes—a signature of Miró's fashion label La Veste, which she cofounded with Maria de la Orden (who was also in attendance). "What about stripes?" Miró recalled asking Satloff. "Stripes are really hard to do in jewelry," Satloff explained. The solution was to layer strands of different-colored stones, creating a striped effect when worn together.

Other discoveries were more accidental. Satloff recalled experimenting with two different colorways of earrings before pairing them together on a whim. "It was by accident," she said of the resulting mismatched pair. Miró, meanwhile, has become an unlikely earring convert. "I've never really been an earrings person," she admitted. "But since we designed these, I haven't wanted to take them off!"

The two designers' friendship began in 2018, when Satloff spotted Miró wearing one of her necklaces during New York Fashion Week and reached out over Instagram. They corresponded for years before finally meeting in person last year, when they discovered they were wearing nearly identical arrangements of rings. A shared love of antique jewelry, color, and unconventional styling eventually blossomed into the collaboration.

For the celebration, Hambro Arader oversaw the evening's creative direction, arranging the jewels among frosted fruits, silver serving pieces, and colorful textiles. Later, she moderated an informal conversation between the two designers, which touched on their creative upbringings, shared love of antiques, and the historical techniques behind Larkspur & Hawk. Satloff, a former museum curator, explained how she became fascinated by the Georgian practice of placing thin sheets of metallic or colored foil beneath gemstones to enhance their color and luminosity. The foil itself, she explained, was rather like "a candy wrapper" beneath the stone. Which might explain why the finished pieces look so deliciously irresistible!

#6647. Move Over, Bearista: Panera Has New Limited-Edition Snowman Cups For The Holidays

Just when you thought you had enough cute drinkware to last a lifetime.

Starbucks' Bearista cups have already proved that people will go to some pretty extraordinary lengths for an adorable drinking vessel. We're talking painfully early lines, instant sellouts, and resale prices that might make you reconsider how much you really need another piece of glassware.

Now Panera Bread wants in on the fun. Only instead of a cuddly bear, the bakery-cafe is going with another winter favorite, the snowman. And wouldn't you know, there's even a chance to snag one for free.

On December 3, Panera will be giving away its new glass Snowman Cups with qualifying purchases at participating locations. There's one rather important detail, though: Each cafe will have only 12 available for the promotion. Not exactly a generous supply, and something tells me these won't be sitting around collecting dust for very long.

There are two designs to collect, although which one you'll end up with is anyone's guess, as they're packaged in mystery boxes and the reveal comes after you've already gotten your hands on one.

If you're not interested in competing for a freebie, there's another way to get your hands on one. Panera will also sell a limited quantity through its online shop for $25 each, plus tax and shipping.

And if you're making a Panera run anyway, you might as well check out what's new on the holiday menu. The chain is introducing Peppermint White Mocha and Pistachio White Mocha, each available as a latte, iced coffee, or Frozen Java. The iced coffees get sweet cream cold foam, while the lattes and frozen drinks come with whipped cream. You'll also find peppermint bark or pistachio pieces on top, depending on which flavor you choose.

The new drinks and treats are available at Panera locations nationwide starting this week. As for the Snowman Cups, I can't say whether they'll cause the same frenzy as Starbucks' beanie-wearing bear—but I have a feeling those freebies will melt away pretty damn fast.

#6645. Cranberry Meringue Pie

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling)

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

#6644. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

#6642. Revisiting Jeans and Tees on the Red Carpet, Inspired by the 2027 Met Gala Theme

The 2027 Met Gala theme has officially been announced! Next year, the annual Costume Institute exhibition—titled “extraORDINARY: fashion and the poetics of the everyday”—will ask its visitors “to see the everyday anew,” and will be entirely devoted to celebrating familiar garments and commonplace materials.

The showcase will be separated into two sections: One focused on elevated “archetypal garments,” such as jeans and T-shirts, and the other on garments made of humble and “disposable” materials, including everything from paper to plastic.

While the official 2027 dress code has yet to be announced, it’s an intriguing proposition to strip things back, given the Met red carpets typically lean toward the more extravagant (especially the 2019 Camp year). What can one expect to see celebrities wearing on the iconic Met steps? Jeans and tees will likely have a huge presence on the step and repeat—and past red carpets have proven that A-listers can transform the everyday staples into high-fashion moments.

The simple tee has had many standout moments this year, for starters. Take Zendaya, who rocked a vintage $35 Spider-Man T-shirt earlier this year while promoting her latest installment in the franchise. Wearing it as a dress and pairing it with a pointy white Louboutin pump? Instant fashion serve. Further back in 1999, Liv Tyler and Stella McCartney also both hit the Met Gala in matching “Rock Royalty” tees—turning the simple graphic top into a bold, cheeky statement. You can get abstract with it, too: Charli XCX’s 2024 Met Gala gown, by Marni, was made of patchworked T-shirts.

Jeans, too, have been elevated and transformed on the red carpets. This year, model Bhavitha Mandava wore Mathieu Blazy’s Chanel—her beige muslin half-zip sweater worn over a pair of muslin-printed pants that had a blue jean effect. A fancy-fied, couture jean! Troye Sivan also wore head-to-toe Prada, including a light-wash pair of jeans that served as an homage to the artist Robert Mapplethorpe and his distinct personal style. Jeans, it turns out, can have just as much of a dramatic effect as a ball skirt or suit trouser; It’s all in the storytelling and styling approach.

So, will the 2027 Met Gala unearth some unexpectedly chic jeans and tees moments? You can definitely count it. And if celebrities need some inspiration, fear not: Below, revisit even more of the best jeans and tees moments on the red carpets over the years.

#6638. Buttered Nut Squash

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

#6637. Simkhai Pre-Fall 2027 Menswear

As a designer mainly based in Los Angeles, Jonathan Simkhai can’t help but be influenced by the California coast: It’s in his fashion DNA. But if you think that means board shorts and flip-flops, think again. His pre-fall menswear fuses a free-spirited West Coast sensibility with a little more refinement—alternating between structure and ease. “We started with our great wardrobe heroes, and really played with color and fit,” he said.

Simkhai has been steadily building his menswear business these past few seasons, and his new assortment continued its focus on easy sportswear. Classic red polo sweaters were given sailor collars, and paired with his sleek pleated “Elvis” trousers. His blue-and-white striped polos were updated in cashmere-cotton blends that were soft to the touch. More technical windbreakers, a trending piece, were offered in subtle black and white or punchy red—the perfect thing to wear if you own a sailboat, and want to spend a day at sea. (One can dream.)

If things started to feel too coastal, Simkhai roughed them up with a bit of edge. The standout outerwear was a black funnel-neck leather jacket, boxy and with a sheen finish. Simkhai also offered luxurious suede button-up shirts that are great for those not-too-hot, not-too-cold days. His take on a classic denim jacket, meanwhile, was cropped and given a more nipped waistline.

#6636. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. 2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6633. BA’s Best Pumpkin Pie

This pumpkin pie recipe has converted more than a few pumpkin pie skeptics. It’s the kind of Thanksgiving dessert readers return to year after year—and not just on the holiday. The filling is silky and rich, deftly spiced with cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg, and cloves, and tastes unmistakably of pumpkin.

Sweetened condensed milk and a splash of heavy cream give the custard its velvety texture, while maple syrup and vanilla add depth. We use canned pumpkin purée (Libby’s is our pick) for its consistent texture and concentrated flavor. A blind-baked crust, finished with an egg wash, keeps things crisp underneath all that creamy filling.

The trickiest part is knowing when to stop baking. Look for slightly puffed, set edges and a center that still jiggles gently, like Jell-O. The filling will firm up as the pie cools, giving you smooth, custardy slices. Serve with a generous dollop of whipped cream.

Make it the finale in a classic Thanksgiving feast →

Sure. We tested this very filling in several store-bought pie crusts, with good results. Use an unbaked 9" pie shell and blind-bake it according to the package instructions before adding the filling. Packaged crusts may bake faster than homemade dough, so don’t automatically follow the crust-baking times in this recipe.

Yes. This recipe calls for 2 cups unsweetened pumpkin purée. A standard 15-oz. can contains about 1¾ cups, so you’ll need to open a second can. Save the leftovers for another of our favorite pumpkin purée recipes. And be sure you’re buying plain pumpkin purée, not canned pumpkin pie filling, which already contains sugar and spices.

Bake the pie up to a day ahead, let it cool completely, then wrap and refrigerate until you’re ready to serve. For longer-term planning, you can freeze the baked pie for up to 3 months.

2 hours (plus 4 hours 30 minutes for chilling)

Preheat oven to 425°. Roll out 1 disk Perfect Pie Crust on a lightly floured work surface to a 14" round. Transfer to a 9" pie dish. Pick up edges and allow dough to slump down into dish, letting excess dough hang over dish. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Fold overhang under; pinch and crimp. Chill 30 minutes.

Line dough with parchment paper or foil, leaving some overhang. Fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake until crust is dry around the edges and just beginning to brown, 25–35 minutes. Carefully remove parchment and weights and reduce oven temperature to 350°. Lightly beat 1 large egg, room temperature, in a small bowl just to blend, then brush over inside of crust (not the crimped edges) and continue to bake until crust is set and beginning to lightly brown in the center, 10–15 minutes. Transfer to a wire rack and let cool.

Do Ahead: Crust can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and store at room temperature.

Preheat oven to 325°. Lightly beat 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, and remaining 2 large eggs, room temperature, in a clean small bowl just to blend. Whisk ⅓ cup (67 g) sugar, 1 tsp. ground cinnamon, ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ½ tsp. ground ginger, ¼ tsp. ground cloves, and ¼ tsp. ground nutmeg in a large bowl until no clumps remain. Add egg mixture, 2 cups unsweetened pumpkin purée, ⅔ cup sweetened condensed milk, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. maple syrup, and 2 tsp. vanilla extract and whisk until smooth. Pour into cooled crust. Bake pie until edges are set and slightly puffed but center is recessed and wobbles like Jell-O, 60–75 minutes (it will continue to set after baking). Transfer to a wire rack and let cool at least 3 hours before slicing. Serve with whipped cream.

Do Ahead: Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and chill. Serve warm or at room temperature. You can also freeze pumpkin pie up to 3 months in advance.

#6631. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6630. Brownie Batter Bark

Recipe by Molly Allen, Hood River, Oregon

This egg-free brownie batter bark is quick and easy, and tastes just like brownie batter straight from the bowl.

When I’m making brownies, I always want to swipe my finger against the edge of the bowl and taste the brownie batter. The problem? While it’s delicious, brownie batter contains raw eggs and raw flour, which can make you sick. When you want to lick the spatula but don’t want to risk food poisoning, this brownie batter bark recipe is the perfect solution.

Line a 15x10x1-inch baking sheet with parchment paper.

In a large bowl, combine almond flour, brown sugar, cocoa powder and salt. Stir in the melted coconut oil and vanilla extract until the mixture is smooth.

Spread the mixture on the prepared baking sheet into an even layer. Freeze it for 20 minutes.

Meanwhile, in a small microwave-safe bowl, microwave 1 cup of chocolate chips in 30-second increments until they’re melted, stirring between the intervals. Spread them over the frozen base. Sprinkle the bark with the remaining 1/2 cup of chocolate chips.

Freeze the bark for one hour or until it’s firm. Break it into pieces.

Brownie batter bark is best stored in a zip-top bag or airtight container in the freezer. The cold freezer temperature will keep the bark hard, and provides the best texture when you pull out a few pieces to enjoy. Keep the bark stored in the freezer for up to two months.

This is a great make-ahead potluck dessert. Make it any time, and then store it in the freezer. Grab a few pieces at a time, or serve a whole platter to a crowd.

No almond flour on hand? You can swap in all-purpose flour, but keep in mind the texture may not be the same. If you use all-purpose flour, it should be heat treated before consuming raw.

Spread the flour on a baking sheet and heat it in a 400ºF oven for about five minutes or until it reaches an internal temperature of 160º. Then add it to the dry ingredient mixture.

This recipe calls for unsweetened cocoa powder to deliver deep chocolate flavor. Semisweet chocolate chips are used for the melted chocolate topping for a balance of sweetness. It’s best to stick with semisweet chocolate for a more robust flavor (as opposed to milk chocolate).

You can melt chocolate either in the microwave or over a double-boiler on the stove top. Heat the chocolate slowly on low heat for the smoothest consistency.

The promise of AI automation to fix the administrative problems facing universities is a fallacy. These systems will only increase the burdens of already-struggling institutions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Universities are at a critical point as students and faculty embrace the use of AI. Already, universities like Harvard are introducing courses that feature an AI avatar as an "instructor."

The promises AI offers higher education are familiar: an increase in efficiency as a consequence of less administration, more teaching coverage, better feedback and smarter assessment. But introducing artificial intelligence (AI) systems in an attempt to fix these problems is not the answer. If anything, AI systems will magnify and speed up the bureaucracy that is driving universities' decline.

In practice, the more likely outcome is darker: AI will not simply sweep away the bureaucratic machinery of universities; it will give that machinery a new regime of AI compliance — more policies, more forms, more trackers, more oversight roles and more work downloaded onto faculty who are already stretched thin.

The danger is not that AI will destroy universities but that universities will use AI to preserve the very processes that make them dysfunctional. If this happens, we might see faculty spending less time on research, less time on teaching, and more time on activities that do not directly contribute to the production of knowledge and education of students.

This is already evident in the existing assessment system in the U.K., but shades are creeping into systems elsewhere, providing a window into the future for U.S institutions. A single piece of student work may pass through a plagiarism-detection platform, a grading interface, a moderation spreadsheet for faculty to share feedback, a grade-transfer system, and an exam-board record. Each stage generates its own logins, deadlines, exception rules and audit trails. None of this is inherently malicious. Anonymous marking, moderation, appeals, accessibility and academic integrity are legitimate concerns. But when each concern is implemented as a separate system, the combined effect is administrative incoherence.

In essence, faculty become the human interface between incompatible platforms, spending their time reconciling grades and chasing missing evidence rather than teaching. While this example pertains to U.K. universities, the trend to expand the administrative staff extends to North America. AI simply introduces a new opportunity to increase administration.

AI could, in principle, solve this. It could integrate systems, automate routine reporting, draft feedback, identify inconsistencies and remove duplicate data entry. Yet the institutional incentive is rarely to remove work; it is to make work visible. A university that automates a broken workflow does not necessarily simplify it. It may simply produce faster reports about the broken workflow, more sophisticated dashboards and more elaborate evidence of compliance. The bureaucratic impulse survives by changing its vocabulary: risk management, assurance, transparency, governance, responsible innovation.

At least one possible outcome is that universities will create AI-use policies, require module-level AI statements, mandate disclosure forms, introduce approved-tool lists and establish review committees. Faculty will be asked to redesign assessments, monitor suspected misuse, document their decisions, complete training, and explain their approach to students. Much of this labor will be invisible. It will appear not as a new job title but as an additional expectation attached to teaching.

When something goes wrong, the academic is exposed; when the system works, the institution claims the credit. That asymmetry is corrosive.

That asymmetry is corrosive. It teaches committed staff that careful judgment is not valued as expertise but rather as a compliance risk to be managed, and the consequences will fall unevenly. Experienced faculty, after voicing their concern to no avail, may leave, retire early or disengage. Early-career academics, already precarious because they don't have tenure, will have the least power to resist. Students will receive less of the resource that matters most: sustained intellectual attention.

One possible outcome is that universities will encourage the development of faculty AI avatars and cut hours and employment. The institution will then justify hiring more ‪—‬ not fewer ‪—‬ compliance and "educational enhancement" staff to manage and maintain these AI avatars, negating the idea of efficiency and cost savings. In this scenario, bureaucracy will expand to manage the problems created by its own expansion while undercutting quality for the students who are paying high tuition fees. One might need to hire staff for oversight of these avatars, administrators and lawyers to manage licensing agreements, quality control staff in case things go wrong, and IT teams for integrating them into learning platforms and websites.

There is an alternative to the administrative tasks. AI should be governed by a simple institutional rule: no new compliance requirement without the removal of an equivalent existing burden. If a university requires assessment redesign to accommodate AI, or the introduction of new technology, it should provide protected time, technical support and a single integrated platform. If it expects faculty to manage AI use, it must give them clear institutional backing rather than leaving them to improvise. And critically, it should show how the technology makes work more efficient before rolling it out across the board.

But the deeper issue is not technology but institutional purpose. A university exists — or should exist — to cultivate understanding, judgment and intellectual independence. If its systems consume faculty time, fragment the student experience, and reward documentation over learning, then AI becomes another instrument of managerial self-preservation. The question is not whether universities can adopt AI. It is whether they can resist using AI to automate their own absurdities.

If they cannot, the outcome will be an educational system that looks progressively sophisticated while becoming increasingly hollow ‪—‬ full of monitoring, low on trust; rich in measuring, poor in teaching; obsessed with compliance, indifferent to the people who make education possible; overly procedural sans intellectual life. It will become an audited theater of learning not worth students' time.

A woman's unexplained abdominal pain led doctors to a diagnosis that has only been documented a few hundred times over the past 400 years.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The patient: A 42-year-old woman in Somaliland, Africa

The symptoms: The woman went to the hospital after having three years of chronic, dull pain in her lower abdomen, as well as a growing sense of heaviness in her abdomen that had worsened in recent months.

When doctors reviewed her medical history, they learned that, three years earlier, she had experienced a number of symptoms that seemed to indicate a pregnancy. She recalled her abdomen growing over time and feeling "fetal movements," her doctors noted in a report of the case. Then, the movements stopped, the abdominal growth halted, and the enlargement gradually subsided. She had not sought medical care during or after this apparent pregnancy.

What happened next: When doctors physically examined the woman's abdomen, they found a hard, irregular mass that extended to her belly button and barely moved when they touched it. Blood tests showed mild anemia, meaning she had fewer healthy red blood cells than normal. Her white blood cell count and kidney and liver tests were normal, and a pregnancy test was negative.

An ultrasound revealed a calcified mass and an empty uterus. Calcification is a buildup of calcium that hardens tissue into a solid mass.

To get a better look at the mass, which occupied the woman's lower abdomen and pelvis, the doctors ordered an advanced CT scan to create a 3D model. The imaging revealed that the mass contained clearly identifiable fetal skeletal structures, including a skull, a spinal column, ribs, and arm and leg bones. The mass measured roughly 7 by 5 inches (18 by 13 centimeters).

The diagnosis: Doctors concluded that the woman had a lithopedion, or "stone baby." The term comes from the Greek words "lithos," meaning stone, and "paidion," meaning child.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a typical pregnancy, an egg is fertilized in a fallopian tube — the structure between the ovaries and the womb — and then travels into the uterus, where it implants in the uterine lining. By contrast, lithopedions most often start as abdominal pregnancies,‬ a type of ectopic pregnancy in which the embryo instead implants on the lining of the abdominal cavity.

There, the embryo shares the space with organs like the stomach, kidneys and appendix. These misplaced pregnancies are almost never viable and are highly life-threatening for the mother. Because the placenta attaches directly to delicate abdominal organs and blood vessels, these carry a severe risk of catastrophic internal bleeding.

If the fetus dies at a developmental stage when it is too large for the mother's body to naturally break down and absorb, her immune system can sometimes treat the retained tissue as a foreign object. To protect the mother from inflammatory complications and infection, the body progressively deposits calcium over the fetal remains, creating a protective casing. In this case, the calcified fetus likely accounted for the woman's chronic abdominal pain and increasing sense of heaviness, her doctors concluded.

The treatment: The doctors performed abdominal surgery to completely remove the calcified fetal mass from the woman's pelvis.

The day after surgery, she developed a mild fever and nausea, but both resolved with treatment. She remained stable and improved during her hospital stay before being discharged in good condition.

Follow-up visits over the next six months showed she had healed well, with a complete resolution of her abdominal pain.

What makes this case unique: Only about 340 cases of lithopedion have been documented in the medical literature over the past 400 years, with the earliest documented in 1582.

This woman's case stands out because she was 42 years old, while many recent cases have been diagnosed in postmenopausal women. (Women typically experience menopause around 51 to 52 years old.) In these cases, the initial ectopic pregnancy occurred during the woman's childbearing years, but she unknowingly carried the calcified remains for decades before developing symptoms. For example, a 74-year old woman from India carried her "stone baby" for more than three decades. By contrast, the woman's recent case was caught after only three years.

The case also highlights the challenges of maternal healthcare in resource-limited settings such as Somaliland, where a lack of access to routine prenatal care and early pregnancy scans can lead to delayed diagnoses. That said, the successful use of advanced 3D imaging and complete surgical recovery demonstrate that excellent outcomes are possible even in these constrained environments, the doctors noted.

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6623. Simple-Is-Best Stuffing

More than a decade after Victoria Granof introduced this classic Thanksgiving stuffing recipe, it remains a staff and fan favorite. As former test kitchen director Carla Lalli Music puts it, it’s “everything you want about stuffing—straight down the middle.”

The recipe earns its name: buttery bread, sautéed onions and celery, and plenty of fresh herbs, with no unnecessary extras. Irregular, torn pieces of crusty bread create craggy edges that turn golden and crisp, while the broth-and-egg mixture renders the tender, custardy middle. Fresh parsley, sage, rosemary, and thyme (sing it with us) bring familiar holiday flavor, backed by a generous amount of butter.

Homemade turkey stock is welcome, but good low-sodium chicken broth from a carton works well. (Or use vegetable broth to make this stuffing vegetarian.) Get the first bake out of the way a day ahead, saving the browning for just before dinner.

Pair it with the rest of our classic Thanksgiving menu →

Choose a sturdy, crusty loaf, such as pane Pugliese, a French white boule, or a country-style sourdough. Skip soft sandwich bread, which can turn mushy once the broth goes in. Weigh out 1 lb. before drying it—the 10-cup measurement is approximate—and don’t skip drying the torn bread in a low oven, even if your loaf is already a day old.

Why bake the stuffing covered, then uncovered?

The covered bake cooks the stuffing through while retaining moisture; the uncovered bake gives you a crisp, golden top. The interior should be tender and cohesive, not dried out. Keep an eye on the stuffing during the second bake rather than assuming it needs the full time. The finished stuffing should be golden and crisp on top and reach 165°F in the center.

Yes. Bake it covered up to three days ahead, until the center reaches 165°F, then let cool briefly and refrigerate within 2 hours. Save the uncovered browning step for serving day. Return the stuffing to a 350°F oven, uncovered, until crisp on top and 165°F in the center, about 45–60 minutes. For longer-term prep, follow our guide to making and freezing stuffing ahead.

What’s the difference between stuffing and dressing?

Stuffing usually refers to a mixture cooked inside a turkey, while dressing is baked separately—but plenty of cooks use the names interchangeably. We prefer versions cooked outside the turkey for the crisp top and edges, but feel free to call it whichever name you grew up using.

Looking for a different take? Try our Sausage-and-Herb Stuffing, Cornbread Dressing With Sausage and Corn Nuts, or any of our other favorite homemade stuffing recipes.

Preheat oven to 250°. Grease a 13x9x2" baking dish with unsalted butter and set aside. Scatter 1 lb. good-quality day-old white bread, torn into 1" pieces (about 10 cups), in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet. Bake, stirring occasionally, until dried out, about 1 hour. Let cool; transfer to a very large bowl.

Meanwhile, melt ¾ cup unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat; add 2½ cups chopped yellow onions and 1½ cups ¼" slices celery to melted butter. Stir often until just beginning to brown, about 10 minutes. Add to bowl with dried bread; stir in ½ cup chopped flat-leaf parsley, 2 Tbsp. chopped fresh sage, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh rosemary, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh thyme, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. freshly ground black pepper. Drizzle in 1¼ cups low-sodium chicken broth and toss gently. Let cool.

Preheat oven to 350°. Whisk 2 large eggs and remaining 1¼ cups low-sodium chicken broth in a small bowl. Add to bread mixture; fold gently until thoroughly combined. Transfer to prepared dish, cover with foil, and bake until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center of dressing registers 160°, 35–40 minutes.

Uncover dressing; continue to bake until set and top is golden brown and crisp, 35–45 minutes longer.

Do ahead: Dressing can be baked (before browning) 1 day ahead; uncover and let cool, then cover and chill. Uncover and bake until top is golden brown and crisp, 45–60 minutes.

Leftover stuffing? Use it up in our Winter Panzanella With Stuffing Croutons →

#6622. Have Yourself A Chrissy Little Christmas

Chrissy Teigen is trading a picture-perfect holiday for homemade ornaments, flour-dusted counters, and a verrry full house.

Christmas for Chrissy Teigen, cookbook author and founder of the food and bakeware brand Cravings by Chrissy Teigen, means getting the whole crew together: her husband, award-winning artist and producer John Legend; their four kids; three dogs; a bearded dragon; and a parrot. There’s a lot going on under one roof.But Chrissy handles chaos with ease. These days, she’s more focused on making memories with Luna, 10, Miles, 8, Esti, 3, and Wren, 3, than on making everything perfect.Much of that joy happens in the kitchen, where Chrissy has built a career writing three best-selling cookbooks and launching a line of baking mixes in unexpected flavors, like snickerdoodle with miso-honey sugar.The family travels often, but Chrissy is looking forward to staying put this winter. It’ll give her more space to embrace the spontaneity she’s craving this year—the kind you can find only when you’re home for the holidays.

Chrissy Teigen: Oh, Halloween. We have a big kids’ Halloween party here at the house. We pick a theme and run with it. This year we picked Coraline.

We love crafting so much. I wanted to stay home for the holidays this year because I need all my children to start hand-making their ornaments and putting them on the tree. I’ve entered this time in my life where I want Christmas to be completely whimsical and over the top. I want to have a cute, colorful, chaotic Christmas this year. I want to thread the popcorn onto the string and have the most chaotic kids’ Christmas tree ever. And I can’t wait for that.

Cooking, of course. Scalloped potatoes in my house are very, very holiday. And my mom comes to town. She lives in Thailand, so we love getting the whole family together. And there’s a lot of football. John’s family loves it, and there’s usually a big Ohio State game around Thanksgiving that they all go crazy for. They go just as nuts for the Christmas game, too. It’s very much the whole family on the floor of my house, watching everything together, and it’s beautiful.

It will be filled with so much joy, but it’s going to be an emotional one for me, of course. To have that big yellow chair that my dad loved so much, empty...I don’t exactly know what to expect from me emotionally, but I can imagine it will be all the things that make the holidays so complex: sad and wonderful and special all at the same time.We will bake, with love, the potatoes Dad loved so, so much. We will clean the greens the way Granny (on John’s side) told us to. I’m sure our eyes will well up. It’ll be a testament to how much they meant to us all.

It is, but that recipe has always haunted me. My mom is impossible to get a recipe from. I think a lot of moms do this on purpose: You ask them to share a recipe, and something’s missing, or they leave out one little thing.I’ve checked in about this one so many times. She’s made it twice a year my whole life, and every time I ask about a detail—whether she uses MSG or when she adds the pepper—I get a different answer. So I’m not even sure I have the right recipe in my cookbook. Whenever she makes it, something is different. You could call it a mom’s touch, but I think she’s leaving out an important ingredient because she wants hers to be the best.

We do Tyler Florence’s beef Wellington every year. It looks impressive, but it’s quite simple, and it’s never gone wrong for me. When I cut into it, the color is beautiful, and it’s juicy. Over the years, I’ve learned how to keep the pastry crisp, even on the bottom where the meat juices collect. It’s a flawless recipe, and the peppercorn sauce is amazing. It pleases everyone, and the kids can cut shapes out of the puff pastry. For sides, we have the scalloped potatoes, green beans, and carrots.

My girls are always in the kitchen with me—I’m not allowed to cook without them. I love it, even though it slows things down. Esti is kind of the boss of the house right now, and she gets nervous that if she goes upstairs to shower, we’ll finish the recipe without her. We make sure she’s back in time to cook the recipe from beginning to end. I expect Esti and Luna will do most of the cooking for Christmas dinner.

No, they’re more likely to spill things. The living room is always covered in spills. I often put my drink on the floor because the table is too far away, and the boys knock it over with their feet.

Miles is our “won’t eat anything” guy. He’s eight now, and he’s been picky since he started eating solid food. He mostly likes chicken nuggets, fries, hamburgers, and pizza. Esti’s tastes change quickly. She might want apples with every dinner, then decide she doesn’t like them—and be like, “I never liked apples. Are you crazy?”Wren is our tank. He’ll eat anything. He gets almost catatonic when he’s eating, so he forgets it could make him sick.Luna knows how to make foods taste better. If something has a burnt corner, for example, she’ll cut it off or find another way to improve it. I think that’s really special.

I remember not liking raw tomatoes or avocados when I was young, even though I love them now, so I’m not too worried about how the kids’ tastes will change. They’re kids, and they’re told what to do all day. Food can be one way they speak up and feel like their opinions matter. I get that—it must be hard to be told what to do from morning to night. As long as they’re full and not waking up hungry, I’m fine.

Christmas morning is an all-day experience for us. Once my kids open a present, they want to play with it, so they take their time instead of rushing through the gifts. I used to have so many rules and run around stressing about the wrapping and recycling. Now I just relax and let the day unfold.

I love prepping for Christmas the night before, especially when it’s a secret, and I’m in charge. I’ll make hot cocoa bombs. In the morning, the kids just have to pour hot milk over them. And we’ll have pancakes, bacon, and Mrs. Butterworth’s syrup, get a sugar rush, and then hopefully have like a nice midday crash together.

Luna has always wanted to be in on the secret. I worried that, as my oldest, she might feel like she was missing out on the Christmas magic, but she loves helping make it special for her younger siblings. Last year, I asked if she wanted to stay up all night with me, and she loved that more than anything.She and Esti also love making stockings for the dogs, the bearded dragon, and now the parrot. We had lots of animals growing up, and I remember my mom taking me to PetSmart to pick out little gifts for our bird. I made sure every beating heart in the house got celebrated, and now the kids love doing that, too.

The bearded dragon toy industry is small. Last year we got little inflatable pools, and there are dried insects, as gross as they are. And a little Santa hat. He’s happy with that. I used to make bird toys with my dad for our parrot, so getting things for Audrey reminds me of that time with him.

Without a doubt, and I’m putting Luna in charge. Carrot cake is our family’s favorite. It was my wedding cake, and it’s John’s family’s favorite, too. There’s so much warmth in it: It has spices and real carrots, and it’s sticky, decadent, and delicious. It’s our holiday pleaser.In addition to our carrot cake kit, I hope we can one day offer a kit with lots of elements for people to decorate a cake and have fun with. The holidays are all about slowing down and getting your hands into something, and it doesn’t hurt if you can eat it after, too.

No, but I loved baking mixes, especially confetti cake mix. My dad had a big sweet tooth, and baking mixes and TV dinners were important to me. My mom’s food seemed too spicy or daunting when I was a kid, so my dad and I bonded over Hungry-Man dinners, Kid Cuisine, and Hot Pockets. Homemade food was mostly for the holidays.I think that’s why grocery stores still excite me. I take my kids shopping and love seeing what’s new—and finding foods that taste just like I remember, like frozen Salisbury steak. Those were the foods I grew up on, and I wanted to recreate them at home for my Cravings cookbooks. I’ve never looked down on those foods. They’ve stood the test of time for a reason. They’re nostalgic and wonderful.

#6621. Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.
