#6600. What My Job Is Like as a Fact Checker at Bon Appétit

It takes a village to publish a magazine—and website and app and Youtube channel and more. Phew! Today we’re introducing you to Bon Appétit’s research director Ryan Harrington.

For the non-journalists out there: What does research and fact-checking actually mean?

At Bon Appétit, every story or recipe goes through multiple edits. After that, it’s eligible for research review. At that stage, there are a few major things my team and I look out for:

Information accuracy: This includes checking the spelling of names and brands, making sure descriptions of restaurant menus and dishes are up to date, reviewing the credibility of the sources we point to, verifying portrayals of quoted individuals, and anything else to make sure that when you read a Bon Appétit story, you know it’s true.

Cultural sensitivity: For a long time, food media has been dominated by a certain privileged perspective. This perpetuated a system that sort of relived the Age of Explorers, with people “discovering” new foods and pigeonholing or exotifying other cultures. A big part of research is honoring different experiences—giving people a platform without making it a spectacle.

Legal concerns: The research department is a bridge between our actual legal team and the editorial team. We keep an eye out for things like libel issues, copyright infringement, food safety risks, protecting sources, or anything else that might need to be discussed with lawyers.

And for the aspiring journalists: How do you become a fact checker? What did you do before joining the Bon Appétit team?

I finished undergrad with a bachelor’s degree in chemistry and then spent six years managing operations of a thoracic surgery laboratory, studying forms of lung cancer. I reached a point in that career where I was asked to go back to school for a master’s or a PhD. I realized if I were to invest all of my time in further education, I wanted to study something I felt really strongly about. And that was food media.

I entered the NYU Food Studies master’s program with the goal of studying the cultural impacts of food media. Early on, I got an opportunity to intern at Food & Wine. During my time there, I was asked to help with other projects beyond my internship, and that’s when I started thinking about food media not as just an academic subject but as a viable career. I eventually started working for other publications like Travel & Leisure and Lucky Peach (RIP).

I also tried working at a brewery, though I had started there in February 2020. Dealing with the development of COVID was maybe not the best time to dip my toe in the industry, but I did get a better understanding of the pandemic’s impact.

When I saw the research director position at BA, I knew my previous experiences and education gave me a strong skill set to lead research efforts, and I am grateful for the opportunity. I’ve now been here five years.

You also teach food studies at NYU. How does that inform your work at Bon Appetit?

Whether I am building a lesson plan or reviewing a story for BA, I always try to understand things from the perspective of the recipient: the students or readers. Are we conveying the story clearly? What are they taking away from it? Guiding people to those light bulb moments, from the classroom to the newsroom, is why I love doing what I do.

It’s so cool that you started a research fellowship program here, so students can get real-world experience in media. Tell us more about that.

As mentioned, I got my start in the industry thanks to an internship. I never had formal journalism or media training, but it was thanks to that program that I could build relevant experience and make connections that opened up a chain of other opportunities. When I started at BA, it was my top priority in being able to pay it forward and help mentor a new generation of passionate food lovers.

I teach them the skills to be a great research editor and also try to give each fellow the freedom to pursue their own interests and network while here. Some fellows have spent time in our Test Kitchen, seeing how we develop and edit recipes. Some have pitched and written great stories and published them on our site. Some have helped our photo team and learned what it means to style a recipe for a shoot. Every fellow has different ambitions and I want them to get the most out of their time working with us and further their own goals.

What are your favorite types of stories to work on here at Bon Appétit? What are the most challenging?

I grew up watching Alton Brown’s Good Eats. Forever a scientist at heart, this influence had a life-long impact, nurturing a desire to understand not just the “how” but the “why” behind cooking, while simultaneously emphasizing creativity, ingenuity, and understanding. So when we take a deep, explanatory dive in processes, like our video on how Dr. Arielle Johnson makes a chocolate bar, that’s where I really feel like I am in my element. (Fun fact: Arielle and I were chemistry lab partners during our freshman year of college at NYU.)

The biggest challenge for me is when we cover wine. It has a lot of specific terminology, strict regulations across international borders to keep straight, and foreign spellings with diacritics that I have to be mindful of. Thankfully, I have built a contact list of passionate and educated people on the subject that I can consult when I inevitably have questions.

What’s the funniest rabbit hole you fell down on a BA research assignment?

We ran a story featuring Moe Girton and her bar Gossip Grill back in 2021. During her interview, she discussed the lesbian bar scene in San Diego when she first moved there in the late ’90s. There was a note from the author of the story to me: “note to fact-checkers to verify the names [of these bars].”

Of the three bars she mentioned, two were relatively easy to track down and confirm. But that third one did not have much of a digital footprint. I was looking through local newspaper archives, old community forums and message boards, and anywhere else that people might have left mention of this bar. Though I found some clues, sometimes pieces contradicted each other, and eventually I reached back out to Moe to see if she could give me any more info.

While she couldn’t remember too many specifics, I was able to get the cross streets of where she thought it was located. So I called businesses in that area, one by one, to see if: (1) They were around in the late ’90s and (2) They remembered a neighborhood lesbian bar nearby. A long shot, but as luck would have it, I eventually spoke with the owner of George’s Camera, a photography store that has been in business since 1965. Right next door to him used to be Patti’s Bar, a business he described as a “lesbian and biker friendly bar.” And the best part? He happened to have a photo of their storefront from back then, signs and all.

What’s the Bon Appétit recipe you make most often?

I absolutely love Shilpa Uskokovic’s French Onion Tart. It always impresses guests because it seems fancy and labor-intensive, but in reality, it’s so hands-off that I can be doing any number of other tasks (or taking it easy!) while it comes together. The deliciousness-to-effort ROI is through the roof. And two sheets of puff pastry in the box means one for the party, one for breakfast the next morning all to myself.

What’s your favorite obscure food trivia?

I am a product of my time and have spent more than my fair share in debates on “What is a sandwich?” But did you know, in New York, “sandwiches are generally subject to sales tax.” And so, the NY Department of Taxation and Finance has a whole page dedicated to what they consider a sandwich. Spoiler alert: They take a pretty broad stance. Hot dog? Sandwich. Burrito? Sandwich. A freaking buttered bagel? Sandwich.

Other parts of the country hold to a tighter definition. In 2006, the Worcester Superior Court of Massachusetts ruled that a burrito is not a sandwich. When a Qdoba opened in White City Shopping Center, an already present Panera Bread tried to enforce a clause in their lease with the mall that barred any competing sandwich shops from opening. After expert testimony arguing the sides of this case, Judge Jeffrey Locke concluded that a burrito is not a sandwich, allowing Qdoba to operate near Panera without violating the lease.

Maybe there isn’t a perfect answer to this question. Maybe the sandwich was really the friends we made along the way.

Can we convince you to apply to Jeopardy?

The great thing about this job is that I don’t need to know the answer to everything. I just need to know how to find who could answer it. And I don’t think Ken Jennings will let me use Google during filming.

How does AI intersect with or influence your current work?

AI is a powerful tool that can synthesize large volumes of data. But in the world of factual accuracy, there are all sorts of caveats and concerns with the content it generates. It’s still too early to safely adopt blanket applications of AI, but there are ways that it can be useful. Early in my career, when I was the bottom rung of the editorial team, I was often asked to transcribe other reporters’ interview recordings. An hour-long interview could easily take two or three times as long to transcribe by hand with my amateur skills. AI transcription services are far from perfect—and I still need to listen to the recording while reading to verify and fix portions—but it is a huge time-saver.

What kitchen tool (or gadget or appliance) are you obsessed with right now?

I love my immersion blender! It can deal with so many tasks in my lovely but small NYC kitchen without needing any valuable countertop real estate. Pasta sauce, soups, salsa, smoothies, it pureés it all and doesn’t even risk any spillage when trying to move things from pot to pitcher and back to pot again.

Special shout-out to chef Frank Proto’s tip to use a pair of tongs to juice citrus fruits too. Used this one recently while on vacation in the rental home’s bare-bones kitchen. From marinades to margaritas, we needed a lot of fresh squeezed juice and this trick really made things easier.

The movie or TV show you’d rewatch until the end of time?

One of my favorite shows is Happy Endings, a modestly successful sitcom that ran on ABC from 2011–2013. It’s a Seinfeld template of a group of friends navigating urban young adulthood. And like Seinfeld, it has characters that are acutely aware of the social games that they must struggle through to be a part of a functioning society.

I actually wrote an academic paper discussing how Happy Endings explores food and gender through its use (and sometimes subversion) of the big eater trope. It is performed across two characters of different genders and sexuality and represents a convergent idea of exactly that—performance. Society has expectations that can seem limiting or at least arbitrary. But when we see these characters act in ways that challenge these social conventions, it is encouragement for us to be able to do so as well.

Archaeologists found several ancient weapons, intact vases and a bronze razor in the volcanic crater lake.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have recovered a well-preserved bronze sword from a volcanic lake in Italy. The 3,300-year-old weapon may have been deposited in the lake as an offering to a deity or for a high-status warrior who lived long before the rise of the Etruscans or the Romans.

The sword was found in Lake Mezzano, which is located in the crater of an ancient volcano roughly 60 miles (100 kilometers) northwest of Rome, according to a translated statement from the Superintendence of Archaeology, Fine Arts and Landscape for the Province of Viterbo and Southern Etruria. Dating to the Late Bronze Age (14th to 13th centuries B.C.), the sword has maintained its sharp edge. It is the third such sword found in Lake Mezzano in the past 50 years.

Bronze Age people erected pile dwellings or stilt houses in what is now Lake Mezzano, and archaeologists recovered parts of the submerged settlement during their recent investigations. According to the statement, researchers also found numerous intact vases, axes, arrowheads, daggers, spearheads, pins and a bronze razor.

The bronze sword dates to the Late Bronze Age and may have been a symbol of power.

The sword and the razor were found near each other, suggesting the two artifacts may have been linked to a person of high social status, such as an elite warrior. But the placement of the metal weapons in a lake may also be related to a wider Bronze Age ritual practice where hoards of jewelry and bent or ritually "killed" artifacts were tossed into bodies of water. This practice continued through the centuries into Etruscan times, when wells were ritually "closed" with artifacts and human sacrifices.

During the 13th century B.C., people in central Italy engaged in trade networks that spanned the Mediterranean. "In this context, bronze weapons were not only instruments of combat, but also symbols of prestige, identity, and power," according to the statement.

The sword and other artifacts discovered in Lake Mezzano are giving archaeologists new information about the people who flourished in prehistoric Italy long before the Romans and Etruscans. Additional research is planned in the coming years, according to the statement.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6596. Dry-Brined Turkey With Tangy Honey Glaze

This dry-brine turkey recipe produces a Thanksgiving centerpiece that’s full of flavor and juicy as heck. The brine is just kosher salt and brown sugar, applied at least 12 hours and up to 2 days ahead. The salt helps the meat retain moisture, while an uncovered rest in the fridge dries the skin for better browning—no bucket required.

Roasting the bird on a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet (instead of a high-sided roasting pan) lets hot air circulate around it, encouraging browning all over. We’ve also done away with the turkey baster in favor of a buttery honey-vinegar glaze you’ll brush over the bird while it cooks. Fragrant with rosemary, garlic, and orange zest, with Worcestershire sauce for savory depth, the repeated brushing builds an even, glossy lacquer.

Let the cooked turkey rest uncovered for 30 minutes to 1 hour before carving. Resist the urge to tent it with foil, which traps steam and softens that hard-earned crispy skin. Use the downtime to put the finishing touches on your Thanksgiving side dishes.

What kind of turkey should I buy for dry-brining?

Choose an unseasoned turkey. Kosher, self-basting, and enhanced turkeys have already been salted, so adding this dry brine can make them overly salty. Check the label for an added salt solution before buying. A frozen turkey is fine; thaw it in the refrigerator for at least 24 hours before starting the brine.

No. In this recipe, the brine stays on the bird; Step 2 calls for rinsing the baking sheet and rack to prevent the drippings from becoming too salty, not the turkey. Follow the measurement for your brand of kosher salt, and don’t feel compelled to use every last grain of the mixture—the recipe intentionally makes extra.

Yes, but taste them first: The dry brine and glaze make these drippings especially flavorful, and they may be quite salty. Skim off the excess fat to make your roux, then add the juices a little at a time, followed by low-sodium chicken broth (or homemade unseasoned turkey stock).

Our Make-Ahead Gravy doesn’t need drippings, but you can stir some in as it reheats. Taste before adding salt.

Can I use a larger or spatchcocked turkey?

Yes, but not with the same roasting schedule. This dry brine recipe is written for a whole 12–14-lb. bird; a larger turkey or one that’s been flattened will cook differently. For a spatchcocked bird, follow our Spatchcock Turkey With Anise and Orange rather than transferring this recipe’s roasting and glazing times.

See why each step works in our guide to cooking Thanksgiving turkey →

4 hours 45 minutes, plus at least 12 hours brining

Place ½ cup Diamond Crystal or ¼ cup plus 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar in a small bowl and work together with your fingers until incorporated. Place one 12–14-lb. turkey, neck reserved for gravy, giblets discarded, on a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet and pat dry with paper towels. (If you don’t have this setup, place your turkey on a V-shape rack set inside a large roasting pan.) Sprinkle salt mixture all over outside of the turkey as well as inside the cavity of the turkey, patting to adhere and nudging some into every crevice. You won’t need all of the dry brine, but it’s good to have extra since some of it will end up on the baking sheet as you season the turkey. Chill bird, uncovered, at least 12 hours and up to 2 days.

Remove turkey from wire rack and rinse baking sheet and rack if needed (turkey will most likely release some liquid onto pan). Line baking sheet with 3 layers of foil and set rack back inside. Place turkey, breast side up, on rack and tuck wings underneath. Let turkey sit at room temperature 2–3 hours.

Place an oven rack in middle of oven; preheat oven to 450°. Using your fingers, loosen turkey skin on breast. Work 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, under skin, spreading evenly over both breasts. Smear outside of turkey with another 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature.

Tie legs together with kitchen twine and pour 1 cup water into baking sheet.

Roast turkey, rotating pan halfway through, until skin is mostly golden brown all over, about 30 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook ¼ cup sherry vinegar or red wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. honey, 4 tsp. Worcestershire sauce, 3 sprigs rosemary, 3 garlic cloves, crushed, two 2x1" strips orange zest, and remaining 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, in a small saucepan over medium heat until bubbling and slightly thickened, about 5 minutes. Reduce heat to lowest setting and keep glaze warm.

Reduce oven temperature to 300° and continue to roast turkey, brushing with glaze every 30 minutes and adding more water by ½-cupfuls as needed to maintain some liquid in baking sheet, until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of breast near the neck registers 155° (don’t worry; the temperature will continue to climb while the bird rests), 65–85 minutes longer. Skin should be deep golden brown, shiny, and crisp. Transfer turkey to a cutting board and let rest at least 30 minutes and up to 1 hour before carving.

#6595. Chrissy Teigen Opens Up About First Christmas Without Her Dad: ‘I Don’t Exactly Know What To Expect’

The holiday will bring a mix of joy and sadness as she honors her father through family traditions.

Chrissy Teigen is known for her candid, filter-free personality and playful, unpretentious comfort food, especially around the holidays. But this Christmas will be different. In an exclusive interview with Delish, the cookbook author shares how she's preparing for her first holiday season without her dad.

Teigen announced the death of her father, Ron Teigen Sr., over the summer in an emotional Instagram post, per People. “Yesterday I woke up with a daddy and went to bed without one,” Teigen wrote in her caption.

In the caption, she described the shock of losing him in the middle of an otherwise ordinary day.

“All the same things happened. Hurried shower. Picked up stuffing from the dog toys. Answered some emails. Avoided some. Laughed with my friends and put on a pretty dress for a friend's birthday. Took a video. How cute is this dress!” she continued. “And then my dad just like...f---ing died.”

She admitted that she wasn’t prepared for how hard the loss would hit.

“I thought that since we talk about it and I’ve come to terms with him always having been an ‘old dad’ that I wouldn't have fallen to the ground the way I did. I’ve thought about this phone call for years. I’ll be ready,” she wrote.

This will be her first Christmas without her father, and Chrissy says it will be emotionally complicated.

“[Christmas] will be filled with so much joy, but it’s going to be an emotional one for me, of course. To have that big yellow chair that my dad loved so much, empty...I don’t exactly know what to expect from me emotionally, but I can imagine it will be all the things that make the holidays so complex: sad and wonderful and special all at the same time.”

Chrissy plans to pay tribute to her dad in part by cooking the scalloped potatoes her family makes every year. “We will bake, with love, the potatoes Dad loved so, so much.”

Chrissy also reflects on other family members they have lost. John Legend’s grandmother, Marjorie Maxine Stephen, passed away in 2021 at 91. “We will clean the greens the way Granny (on John’s side) told us to. I’m sure our eyes will well up. It’ll be a testament to how much they meant to us all.”

John and Chrissy share four children—Luna, 10, Miles, 8, Esti, 3, and Wren, 3—and are looking forward to staying home for the holidays. The kids will have time to participate in one of the family’s favorite activities: crafting. “I wanted to stay home for the holidays this year because I need all my children to start hand-making their ornaments and putting them on the tree,” Chrissy says.

“I’ve entered this time in my life where I want Christmas to be completely whimsical and over the top. I want to have a cute, colorful, chaotic Christmas this year.”

#6594. Copycat Coopers Hawk Red Wine–Braised Short Ribs

This copycat Cooper's Hawk red wine-braised short ribs recipe delivers fall-apart-tender short ribs bathed in a luxurious sauce. It's like dining out in your kitchen.

One taste of the red wine–braised short ribs at Cooper’s Hawk is enough to understand why they’ve remained a bestseller. A generous portion of melt-in-your-mouth braised short ribs is stacked over a mound of buttery whipped potatoes, then drizzled with umami-rich braising liquid. When served with roasted vegetables and garnished with crispy fried onion strings, it’s a plate of comfort food that’s just as much a feast for the eyes as it is for the taste buds.

Whether you’ve been to Cooper’s Hawk and want to recreate the magic at home, or you don’t live near a Cooper’s Hawk location and want to know what all the fuss is about, this copycat recipe belongs on your must-try list. It’s the perfect recipe for chilly days when you want a meal that feels like a warm hug. It’s also impressive-looking and great for feeding a crowd, so keep it in mind as the holiday season approaches.

Cooper’s Hawk Winery and Restaurant is something like a more refined Cheesecake Factory that’s known for its wine rather than its cheesecake. Let me break it down. First, each chain greets diners by showcasing its specialties: Where the Cheesecake Factory has cases of cheesecake, Cooper’s Hawk has a well-appointed wine shop. Second, both are known for extensive menus that span a wide range of global influences and cuisines. Finally, both have a long list of signature dishes (we’ve replicated many Cheesecake Factory copycat recipes over the years) that keep customers coming back. These copycat Cooper’s Hawk red wine–braised short ribs, for example, are an ode to the dish that’s been on the menu since the restaurant opened its very first location in 2005.

Preheat the oven to 425°F. Sprinkle the short ribs with salt and pepper. In an ovenproof Dutch oven over medium-high heat, brown the ribs in oil in batches. Remove the meat and set it aside.

Add the celery, carrot and onion to the drippings, and cook them until they’re tender. Add the garlic, and cook for one minute longer. Add the wine and broth, stirring to loosen the browned bits from the pan.

Return the ribs to the pot. Add the parsley and thyme. Cover the pot and transfer it to the preheated oven. Cook the ribs for 2 hours to 2 hours and 30 minutes or until the meat is tender.

While the ribs are braising, in a small bowl, whisk all the butter ingredients until they’re blended. Transfer the mixture to a sheet of storage wrap, and roll it into a log. Refrigerate the butter until it’s chilled. Unwrap and slice it.

Place the hot mashed potatoes on a serving plate. Top them with the short ribs. Immediately top the ribs with a slice of Dijon butter and french-fried onions. Garnish the dish with additional fresh parsley, if desired.

Store any leftover short ribs in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Enjoy them within four days. Leftovers can be microwaved in a microwave-safe container, or they can be transferred to a Dutch oven and warmed in a 350° oven until they’re heated through.

Braised short ribs freeze like a dream. Store them in a freezer-safe airtight container and freeze them for three to four months. Defrost them completely in the refrigerator before warming them in the microwave or in the oven.

Short ribs are a heavily marbled cut of beef from the lower portion of the rib cage (the same area as the chuck and brisket). They have a robust, beefy flavor but contain a lot of connective tissue, so you need to cook them slowly with low heat for the meat to become tender.

Braising is one of the best (and most popular) ways to prepare short ribs. That said, you can make bone-in short ribs in a slow cooker or on a wood, pellet or charcoal smoker. To speed up the process, you can also make tender bone-in short ribs in a pressure cooker.

Cooper’s Hawk serves their short ribs with mashed potatoes and roasted vegetables, but that is far from the only pairing option. Serve them over a bowl of creamy polenta or on a bed of buttered egg noodles (similar to beef Stroganoff). For freshness, add a garden salad, grilled asparagus or creamed spinach for a more indulgent spin.

Sure! If you want to recreate Cooper’s Hawk braised short rib risotto, prepare this recipe as directed, minus the potatoes, veggies, and onion strings. Instead, saute a blend of mushrooms in a skillet and prepare this parmesan risotto while the short ribs braise in the oven. When everything is ready, shred the short ribs into small pieces and combine them with the mushrooms and risotto. Serve the risotto in shallow bowls with a few spoonfuls of braising liquid and a drizzle of white truffle oil.

#6593. Hasan Minhaj Thinks America’s Greatest Accomplishment Is Cereal

This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people. This interview series dives deep into their food routines, including dinner party strategies, cherished cookbooks, and the memorable bites they’d hop on a flight for.

Comedian and actor Hasan Minhaj is known for quippy questions, biting comebacks, and colorful commentary, but his most delightful soundbites are about food. During a recent  hour-long chat, he named a wide range of favorites, including bananas and oranges (“they come prepackaged and are great for traveling”); macaroni and cheese (“I love every category and version of it, from the box of Kraft to anyone’s Thanksgiving mac ’n’ cheese”); and dal chawal (specifically his mom’s version of the lentils and rice dish, “pure comfort food and my love language”).

These are the best-of-the-best bites for Minhaj, which is coincidentally the name of his new movie—Best of the Best, streaming now on Netflix—that he cowrote and produced with Prashanth Venkataramanujam and stars in as a professor and former dancer. The film pays homage to real-life Bollywood competitions, following collegiate dancers Maya and Anjali (played by Maitreyi Ramakrishnan and Priyanka Kedia, respectively), whose characters were inspired by “deeply passionate college kids in the biggest world that a lot of people have never heard of.”

Fiery passion is at the center of Minhaj’s life, especially when it comes to actual spice. “Some people want to drive at 85, some like a nice even 65, and some take it five miles below the limit,” he explains in a speedy analogy. “My spice level? I want to feel things in all caps. Life is to be lived. So I’m like, ‘Give it to me!’ Give me the full robustness of flavor that’s possible. I am a maximalist and love it all!”

His other spice of life is chai, “a form of commiseration, community, and love in Indian households—and an entry point to gossiping.” He loves that everyone does chai differently (he and his wife, Beena, prefer a more ginger-forward profile, while his parents like it sweeter). That’s why he became an investor and partner in the New York City-based Kolkata Chai in 2024, working with brothers Ani and Ayan Sanyal to expand the reach of a drink so engrained in their lives and culture. “It’s a welcome change to a lot of people’s only chai experience being at Starbucks in Middle America. It’s really amazing how you can change the complete perspective of an entire culture because of a drink that people can explore and make their own.”

Read on for Minhaj’s answers to our Amused Bouche questionnaire—it’s no surprise they’re chock-full of equally heartwarming and appetizing soundbites.

If you could only eat one thing 24/7/365, what would it be?

America is celebrating its 250th-year anniversary, and I think as a country, America’s greatest accomplishment is what we brought to cereal. I have been caught many a time red-handed with my full paw inside of some Golden Grahams, going to town. I will kill half a box, straight up, no milk. It is a snacking cereal. I’ll be watching a prestige drama and stress-eating Golden Grahams. Sometimes I’ll even drizzle honey over a bowl. I’ll also do the same with Honey Bunches of Oats. There’s a Montagues-and-Capulets debate here of blue box or orange box. I’m a blue box guy, because I love the almonds, extra crunch, and sweetness. It was my granola mix before I started eating granola, and it’s like trail mix without dastardly raisins coming in and f—ing shit up!

What’s the first thing you learned how to cook?

A strawberry Toaster Strudel, one of my all-time favorites. I popped it in the toaster as a kid, and it was an eye-opening experience. When I came home from elementary school, it felt like I was a master chef making myself this crisp little strudel cake and frosting it. I felt like a confectionery master. It was incredible. I toasted it on a level three and would sometimes pop it up and flip it midway through.

I actually didn’t hit my growth spurt until much later in high school, so I was quite undersized and malnourished-looking when I was younger. I was bullied a lot. My mother would make me eat three hard-boiled eggs on the way to school. And I hated hard-boiled eggs. Now that I’m a parent of small children, I understand the efficacy of hard-boiled eggs. But now I will pan-fry hard-boiled eggs, because really my hatred of them came from texture and temperature issues. But if you cut them in half and fry them yolk side down, there’s a crispness that makes it turn into a crunchy, almost taco-like topping that you can put on top of bread and butter.

It’s a really delicious, warm-and-gooey snack that I started making when I tried to give my daughter a hard-boiled egg and she immediately spit it out. I’m like, “Yeah, the cycle of torture continues! There needs to be a better way! Let me figure out a way to make this delicious.” The secret was making a quesadilla as the on-ramp she needs to get eggs in her. It was an experiment I worked backward from, kind of like writing a joke, telling a story, or working on a screenplay. My daughter loves quesadillas but hates eggs, so by making it into crunchiness that would blend right in, it wouldn’t feel like a squishy thing that I’m force-feeding her.

Growing up, we were never allowed to order dessert from restaurants. It is my greatest joy to order dessert from restaurants. I’ll tell the missus to order whatever she wants. Sometimes she’ll be indecisive. She always wants the chocolate lava cake, but she’ll be eyeing a berry tart. It’s a distant second, but I’ll take the bullet and order both for us to share. Sometimes when I do it, I’ll look over my shoulder to be like, “Are mom and dad going to find out?” But now I’m dad. We’re mom and dad!

I do not cook from cookbooks, but I will cook from YouTube Shorts. There’s just something about the looping nature of it breaking down the recipe. It’s tickling something in my mind and letting me know, “Hey, it’s not that hard. You can totally do it! You’ll get to completion, and it’s going to look pretty good.” And then as soon as doubt kicks in, the video starts playing again and snaps me out of it. It’s like the feeling of playing a song that you love over and over again, like “This Is How We Do It” by Montell Jordan. Play it again! “Men in Black”—play it again! I want to listen to it again, and that’s the feeling I get when I search “chicken tinga recipe” on YouTube Shorts.

Is there a cooking disaster that made you swear off a dish forever?

My wife does most of the cooking, but I want to put on the record that I try. I do cook, but a lot of the reaction is like, “Oh, you tried. I appreciate the effort. And that’s great for you. Why don’t you enjoy the omelet that you’ve made?” But I think I make a great soft-scramble, and what I bring to the breakfast table is pretty solid. I used to burn all of my food because I got impatient and cranked up the heat too fast. I learned you can’t bring microwave energy to a stove. Once I understood that foundational element in not burning your eggs, it was a huge unlock. Then I got to experience the full variety of eggs that aren’t charred.

Which nostalgic foods from childhood bring you the most comfort?

Dal chalwal: just lentils and rice. It has always been the first thing my mom makes for me when I get home to Sacramento, from college until now. It’s this beautiful gesture of love that I’m eating dal chawal with my mother, and her grandchildren are eating it with her at the same time. It’s pure comfort food and my love language.

When you’re playing dinner-party DJ, what’s spinning?

It’s a seasonal thing. Beena is really the entertainer and has been an incredible host since we met. For a holiday party, she’ll queue up a Pentatonix holiday playlist. Thematic, but a little left of center and unexpected.

What is your biggest entertaining flex to impress guests?

Beena loves a theme. We host Halloween on our block every year and call it Boo Bash. We go all out with a Halloween-themed live band, fog machines on the dance floor—aka the driveway—children’s face painting, bounce house, fake blood as drinks in IV bags. Her level of joy and imagination is unparalleled. She’s incredible. I add pizzazz, but I’m like, “Go off, queen!” She is the show. She’s the show creator, and I’m the showrunner.

Tell me about a meal so good you would hop on a flight to relive it.

My grandparents on both sides of my family have passed away, but I’m lucky enough that I was raised by my grandmother on my mother’s side from third to fifth grade. There’s a specific memory of when my grandmother made biryani. When the lid came off the pot and the steam and aroma of all the flavors escaped for the first time, she would put a ladle in and scoop it out for me, with meat that is so tender because it’s been cooking for so long. That’s the feeling that I would chase and book a flight immediately for, but it’s just a feeling. A feeling of love from it taking all day to make biriyani and that she loved me enough to put in that time and energy. Goat biriyani especially was a special-occasion dish, like when a cousin was getting married, and I associate it with being with family and something happy happening. In Hindi you call it ghar kha khana, the food from home. Biryani is the crème de la crème and the chef’s kiss of Indian cuisine for me. Especially my grandmother’s.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Colorectal cancer in young people shows genetic and structural differences that may make it more aggressive and treatment-resistant than the cancer tends to be in older people.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Colorectal cancer rates have been rising in people under 50 since the mid-1990s. These early-onset cancers tend to be more aggressive and resistant to treatment than cancers in older adults — and now, scientists may be learning why.

A new study published Thursday (Oct. 29) in the journal Nature Medicine compared colorectal tumors from people between 29 and over 90 years old, and it revealed key differences between young and old patients.

The new findings might, in turn, help scientists uncover new ways to fight colorectal cancer in young people, said study co-author Ana Anderson, a professor of neurology at Harvard Medical School and a core faculty member of the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation at Brigham and Women's Hospital.

"I believe that our study is essentially a turning point now in the field," Anderson told Live Science. "Because up until now, we've had more questions than answers."

Many questions surround early-onset colorectal cancer, as the disease is rising in people under 50 even as it falls in older populations. It's now the leading cause of cancer death in the U.S. for people under 50, and its numbers are even on the rise among children and adolescents.

Beyond questions about what's driving this uptick in cases, another mystery has been why this disease is so deadly in young people.

"The clinical data suggests that the disease in the younger patients is more aggressive overall," Anderson said. "The patients, being very healthy otherwise, do not do well with treatment."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The reason why colorectal cancer is often aggressive in younger patients hasn't been clear.

To investigate that mystery, Anderson collaborated with Dr. Kimmie Ng, an oncologist at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, and Dr. Ramnik Xavier, a gastroenterologist at the Broad Institute and Mass General Brigham. They used a method of analyzing RNA in cells that allowed them to work with frozen and banked tumor tissue. RNA, a cousin of DNA, reflects the genes that are active in cells. In all, the team analyzed 189 tumors: 54 from patients under 50 and 135 from patients over 50.

With that many samples, the researchers could look at gradual differences tied to each age group, instead of just comparing tumors between the younger and older groups overall. That enabled them to pinpoint subtle differences, Anderson said.

For starters, younger people had a higher proportion of connective tissue cells in their tumors than they did of malignant cancer cells. That pattern was flipped in patients of older ages. Having a smaller proportion of malignant cells might sound good, but connective tissue in tumors can secrete compounds that suppress the immune system, Anderson said. That helps protect the tumor from immune cells that might otherwise target its cells for destruction.

These connective tissue cells can also physically block chemotherapy drugs from getting to the cancerous cells. This could be one reason younger patients' cancers resist treatment, the researchers suggested.

Based on patterns of gene activity in the tumors, the researchers suspect that younger patients' cancer cells also show distinct activity related to cell-to-cell communication. That may help the cells migrate through the body more easily than cancer cells in older patients do. In other cancers, this kind of gene activity has been linked to more aggressive tumors and a greater chance that the disease will spread, or metastasize, Anderson said.

The study's results also turned up an intriguing mystery: the presence of lots of long noncoding RNA. These strands of RNA contain more than 200 building blocks, called nucleotides, that don't provide instructions for building proteins. Coding RNA, in contrast, is ferried to protein-building factories in cells to be used as blueprints.

Scientists don't know what much of this long noncoding RNA does in the body, nor do they understand what it is doing in the tumors specifically. However, they hope to find out.

Anderson and her team are already working on manipulating the RNA they found inside cancer cells in petri dishes. In time, this line of research could supply another piece of the puzzle, helping scientists understand why colorectal cancer is so aggressive in young people.

"It's a new avenue for research into this disease that we previously had no idea about," Anderson said.

She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

#6591. Harvest Caesar Salad

Caesar salad is a year-round favorite in my kitchen, but this harvest spin is on repeat during the fall. Butternut squash pieces are baked with crispy baked Parmesan frico, turning them into cheesy squash “croutons” that give this classic salad the perfect autumnal spin. Trust me—it’s the Friendsgiving dish that everyone will be requesting next year.

The kale:Raw kale can be aggressive, with a rough, almost squeaky texture, so it’s important to treat it by massaging it with both lemon juice and salt before tossing with the dressing. The combination of acid and salt (and your elbow grease!) works together to partially break down the kale fibers, tenderizing it. Wondering how you go about “massaging” the kale? It’s not a science: You literally pretend the bowl of greens is someone’s shoulders. Put your hands in there and massage away!

The croutons:Similar to my crispy Parmesan potatoes, these frico squash croutons are made by roasting the squash on a bed of shredded Parm. In the oven, the cheese melts and caramelizes on the baking sheet, forming this crunchy, crispy crust underneath the squash. This isn’t a difficult technique, but there are a few tips that will make the process much easier.

Make ahead:The frico squash croutons are best fresh (once refrigerated, they’ll lose their crispness), but the dressing can be made 1 day ahead. The kale can also be destemmed and torn up to 1 day ahead, but wait to massage it with the lemon juice and salt until just before serving.

Did you try making this? Rate and review it below!

#6590. 16 Excellent Restaurants to Try in Nashville

Nashville has long been a haven for aspiring country stars and songwriters, but these days, my hometown is also experiencing a surge in culinary talent. A decade or two ago, finding hand rolls made with fish from Tokyo or natural wine by the glass was a challenge. Now, we’re in business, with more options coming down the pike at a rapid pace.

Born and raised in Nashville, I spent my childhood digging into plates of fried chicken with sides of squash casserole and turnip greens at Elliston Place Soda Shop and meandering out to Highway 100 for a plate of biscuits at The Loveless Cafe—establishments that have fed this city for generations. We’ve always eaten well here, but as the city has changed, so have its tastes, expanding beyond the down-home cooking visitors might expect.

That’s a good thing. Ours is a vibrant dining scene that caters to all tastes and budgets, from experimental fine dining to tried-and-true lunch counters. Use this as your primer to getting a taste of Music City. Whether you’re craving a plate of hot chicken from Prince’s or a piece of freshly butchered bluefin tuna, Nashville has it.

Tucked into an alley attached to the Nashville Arcade lies one of Nashville’s dreamiest new bars, an oasis of blush Italian marble and cocktails that defy convention. The product of chef Julia Jaksic and beverage director Owen Gibler, it offers downtown a much-needed respite from honky-tonks and domestic beers. Gibler uses digestifs and aperitifs to create cocktails that have exceptionally aromatic qualities on the nose and on the palate. Jaksic’s menu of bites is designed to accompany cocktails and conversation. Think gorgeous little snacks like cheesy gougères with spicy ’nduja and fluffy focaccia topped with rich stracciatella and mortadella. The bar has quickly amassed a crowd of regulars and industry pros. Come for the drinks, stay for the impeccable vibes and tunes on an analog reel-to-reel tape player.

Visiting Nashville? Step one: Book your reservation at Kase x Noko, the tiny omakase spot that’s connected to uber-popular Noko. Step two: Book everything else on your trip around that reservation. That’s because this 14-seat sushi counter is one of the hottest tickets in town, offering a 14-course omakase at an unheard of $75 price point. There are ways to ratchet up the bill, of course, with add-ons like “steak and eggs”—nigiri stacked with A5 Wagyu, uni, and caviar—or flame-seared yellowtail belly, expertly formed and presented by chef and co-owner Dung “Junior” Vo and his crew. The playlist is curated by partners Wilson Brannock and Jon Murray, leaning heavily on early-2000s hits, an excellent background for cocktails starring flavors such as shiso, yuzu, and pandan.

What started as a pandemic-era tortilla pop-up quickly blossomed into a very popular food truck, followed by a tortillería, and now a full-service restaurant in the Gulch, serving chef Julio Hernandez’s Tennessee-Mexican dishes. Hernandez, who grew up among Tlaxcala’s corn and cooked his way through New York and Nashville kitchens, serves dishes such as grilled chorizo with heirloom beans, served with collard greens with smoked ham hock, salsa verde, and tortillas, and Tennessee trout with popcorn grits. The heart of it all is the masa that’s nixtamalized in-house using corn from Mexico and, more recently, Tennessee farms. Mezcal and tequila cocktails are thoughtful and plentiful.

Turkey and the Wolf was born in New Orleans, where it became an instant hit for its irreverent vibes and gonzo takes on Southern favorites. Luckily for Nashville, chef-owners Mason Hereford and Lauren Agudo were lured here by its friendly restaurant community, and they teamed up with chef-partner Will Mondros to open the Icehouse in a cinder-block building and covered patio on a scruffy corner lot in East Nashville that was once a dog park. Now, the yard is filled with thrifted tables, an Airstream that serves as the office, and sculptures including a brontosaurus and a life-size rearing horse. The menu includes hits that helped launch Turkey and the Wolf to fame, like the collard melt oozing with slow-cooked greens, Swiss cheese, and Russian dressing, and the towering bologna sandwich stacked with thick slices of fried bologna and a healthy handful of vinegar potato chips. But the Icehouse has its own personality and surprises, including a buttery, flaky roti full of juicy lamb and topped with handfuls of herbs. Specials are constant and often experimental, the beers and cocktails are ice-cold, as the name implies, and there’s often live music in the yard. There’s always a party going on at the Icehouse.

Even if you read the directions closely—“follow the red light”—it may still take you a moment to find the entrance to 888, the Japanese listening room located below the towering JW Marriott, just around the corner from the main hotel entrance. Once inside, the vibes are groovy and the fish is fresh. In fact, diners visiting on the second Saturday of the month will witness master sushi chef Kiichi Okabe breaking down an enormous bluefin tuna, which is then served for immediate, luxurious consumption. Beyond Okabe’s sushi menu, try larger plates like a koji-marinated rib eye cooked over binchōtan charcoal, or the donabe with chicken thighs, mushrooms, and cured egg yolk. The restaurant is styled after a kissa, a Japanese vinyl listening room, and it delivers heavily on that promise with rotating DJs who play soul, funk, disco, and more, as well as full album parties that require silence from the room. Don’t miss out on the Silken Spirit Martini, a tableside service that includes the use of a hand-cranked mechanical shaker to mix Japanese vodka or gin with sake and orange bitters.

2105 Elliston Place, Nashville, TN 37203(615) 219-2704

Aside from hot chicken, Nashville’s other hometown food is the meat ’n’ three, a plate lunch consisting of a protein and three sides. The Southern classic is a specialty of Elliston Place Soda Shop. Opened in 1935, it is one of the few remaining (and best examples) of the genre. Generations of Nashvillians have graced the red leather booths and black-and-white-tiled floors over the years, tended to by a staff that feels like it turns over about once a century. (Ms. Linda, “the pie lady,” still makes her beloved coconut meringue pies every morning.) Though Elliston Place moved to a newer space next door a few years ago, it still features the soda counter and pressed-tin ceiling, which makes the milkshakes and sundaes taste like the good old days.

International Market introduced Nashvillians to Thai food in the 1970s, when it opened on Belmont Boulevard serving an exceptionally affordable steam table lunch of Thai and Chinese dishes. Now, with a new location (across the street) and new ownership (Anna and Arnold Myint, children of the original owners), the restaurant incorporates high-quality local meats and produce in an updated setting—though thankfully the original mustard-and-orange bench seating came along for the ride. The kitchen is now a proving ground for chef Arnold Myint, a James Beard semifinalist. Menu items venture beyond the typical selections of curries with five-spice duck lo mein, shrimp and pineapple curry, and red curry rice ball wraps. At lunch, diners can choose from the classic steam table or order from the menu; nighttime brings table service with Singhas and craft cocktails.

At Locust, chef Trevor Moran created his own culinary genre blending influences from Japan to his native Ireland. I’ve eaten briny Belon oysters that tasted—pleasantly—like licking a battery; a roast sole served with morels and uni; and a bowl of tiny sea snails served with toothpicks and spicy salt. The DIY beef tartare hand rolls—freshly ground bottom round, fluffy rice, and smoky pickled egg cream, plus freeze-dried capers and nori for rolling—are a must, as is the tuna crisp, featuring house-cured slices of tuna loin and belly atop a fried wonton crisp slathered with horseradish. The chefs deliver these dishes to the tables themselves to an eclectic soundtrack featuring everything from Meat Loaf to old-school hip-hop. The drink list is heavy on natural wines, though my go-to is the Toki Highball cocktail or a can of sake. In homage to Moran’s birthplace, there’s also Guinness by the pint, and Irish gin and tonics compete with Orion beer and sake cups.

The diminutive Kisser, modeled after a Japanese kissaten, a neighborhood spot serving comfort food where locals can eat, drink, and hang out, has been a smash hit since opening in 2023. After spending years in some of the best kitchens in L.A. and Nashville, co-owner couple Brian Lea and Leina Horii decided to focus on their own vision. Inspired in part by Horii’s family sushi restaurant in California, the menu blends traditional Japanese cuisine and their fine-dining techniques with dishes like onigiri stuffed with snow crab and avocado, a perfectly crispy chicken katsu sandwich on fluffy housemade milk bread, and bowls of udon in delicate broth. It’s one of the best places in town to enjoy fresh fish, particularly the chirashi bowl brimming with pristine sashimi and glistening salmon roe. Make sure to end your meal with a green melon cream soda or a crackly miso crème brûlée.

Folk is a neighborhood gem that Nashville needs now more than ever as hotels and chains threaten to take hold of the dining scene. The restaurant is perched on a quiet corner in East Nashville’s McFerrin Park and welcomes diners with wood-fired sourdough-crust pizzas—my favorite is adorned with littleneck clams, parsley, bonito, and lemon—and rustic Italian-leaning dishes like Marcella beans with spicy pepper relish, bouncy focaccia with whipped ricotta, and more. From the high-ceilinged dining room, adorned with paper lanterns and exposed-brick walls, you can glimpse the bustling kitchen and blazing pizza oven. Natural wines and classic cocktails are the move at the bar, where the afternoon light streams in during the daily apéro hour. The crowd of shockingly healthy houseplants are as well-nourished as the patrons.

Not far from Folk stands a Tex-Mex taco shop with a sense of humor where you can gobble down one chef’s highly agreeable take on Taco Bell’s Crunchwrap. To make it, chef Bryan Lee Weaver (also of Butcher & Bee) fills his fluffy handmade tortillas with Texas red chili, pork green chili, or both when you order it “Xmas-style.” If tacos are more your speed, you’ll find toppings like brisket, tater tots, and freshly roasted Hatch chiles. To me, the sleeper hit is the vegetarian taco with charred poblano, whipped feta, and crispy rice, thanks to its variety of textures and smoky heat. The queso dip comes with more of those warm, velvety tortillas (never chips!), and the frozen margaritas are tart and free of sickly-sweet sour mix. The interior offers retro-diner vibes, with a Formica bar and red leather booths, but there’s nothing like grabbing a patio seat in the summertime to let those margs work their Texas magic.

Lucky for Nashvillians, former Per Se chef and Nashville native Julia Sullivan came home to open her first solo restaurant in Henrietta Red. This airy, tiled Germantown spot boasts an oyster bar glistening with mollusks, including Maine’s salty Mookie Blues and Alabama’s buttery Murder Points. Despite Nashville’s landlocked status (the Cumberland River doesn’t count), Henrietta Red deftly combines coastal ingredients with Southern flavors in dishes like oysters roasted with ‘nduja butter and whole trout with dandelion greens. Wood-fired seafood is the focus here, but the fresh pastas and vegetables—particularly the beet salad with pistachio and mint—stand out too. Brunch brings its own reason to visit, with dishes like shrimp toast with beets and tahini, and smoked fish cakes with lemon-fennel aïoli.

Despite the ever-widening swath of restaurants serving Prince’s signature dish around the globe, you have to visit the original purveyor to get real-deal Nashville hot chicken. As the story goes, the ultra-spicy sandwich was created as punishment by a jilted lover of Thornton Prince; but, instead of catching on fire, Prince loved the spice so much that he’d go on to perfect the recipe that launched his business. Today, Prince’s remains the best in class, serving up fried chicken spiced with cayenne pepper oil atop a slice of white bread with a pickle (a foil to all that cayenne). If you’re sticking closer to downtown, swing by Prince’s outpost in the Assembly Food hall to get your hot chicken fix.

Wood-paneled walls line the dining room of this classic meat ’n’ three restaurant that’s been serving up Southern soul since 1952. Every day, the fourth-generation owners welcome a regular crowd hungry for roast beef, baked ham, and pit barbecue, plus daily specials like fried catfish, chicken and dumplings, and throwback fixins like candied yams, turnip greens, baked apples, fried corn, and creamed potatoes. Wendell Smith’s is a slice of Nashville that has hung on to its corner lot despite unchecked development all around it, still sharing space with the adjacent liquor store of the same name that’s been operating just as long.

What began 70 years ago as a humble motel and café at the start of the Natchez Trace Parkway has been thriving from the moment Lon and Annie Love began serving biscuits and fried chicken to travelers out of their home kitchen. After their continuing success, the couple turned their home into a restaurant and opened 14 rooms as a motel to accompany their new dining destination. The motel went out of operation years ago, and its rooms are now home to retail space, with smoked hams, jams, and biscuit mix on offer. Though there is now expanded outdoor seating and an outdoor bar serving bloody Marys when the wait is long, there’s nothing better than grabbing a seat in the tiny dining room that still feels like home.

An institution since 1974, this legendary West Nashville steakhouse is a windowless dining room featuring backlit stained glass, carpeting, a stone fireplace with a roaring fire (most nights), and sporty portraits of the hounds and horses that once lived on the grounds of the abutting Belle Meade Mansion. Martinis and Manhattans pair perfectly with Sperry’s steaks and seafood, from a filet Oscar smothered in crabmeat and béarnaise to king crab legs served with drawn butter. Nashville’s very first salad bar remains gloriously intact here, and diners can pile their plate with neon-green goddess and bacon crumbles (though the plated iceberg wedge salad topped with bacon and black olives is my choice). Bananas Foster, another highlight, is served tableside in a plume of booze-soaked flames and cinnamon-fueled sparks. The doors open at four for happy hour, when sausage-stuffed mushrooms and discounted cocktails draw a steady stream of locals each day.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

#6589. Cranberry and Brie Stuffed Chicken

With its savory spinach filling, fruity sauce and gooey cheese topping, this cranberry Brie chicken makes any day a celebration.

Who doesn’t love a recipe that looks like it took hours in the kitchen, but is actually surprisingly easy to pull off? Our Test Kitchen’s cranberry Brie chicken is one of those impressive dinners. Tender chicken breasts are stuffed with a spinach filling, coated in bread crumbs and baked until golden. Then comes the best part: the cranberry sauce topping and slices of creamy Brie that melt right over the top.

With its festive colors and a blend of sweet and savory flavors, this dish is a great choice for Friendsgiving, Christmas Eve dinner or any occasion you want to impress guests. But don’t save it just for company! It’s also a fun way to dress up chicken breasts during the week.

Preheat the oven to 375°F. In a large skillet, cook the onion in oil until it’s almost tender. Add the spinach and garlic, and cook them until the spinach is wilted. Drain any liquid, if necessary. Season the filling with salt and pepper.

Pound the chicken breasts with a meat mallet to 1/4-inch thickness. Divide the spinach mixture among the pieces. Fold the chicken breasts in half, enclosing the filling, and secure them with toothpicks.

Place the bread crumbs and egg in separate shallow bowls. Dip the stuffed chicken breasts into the egg, then roll them in the crumbs to coat them. Place them seam side down in an 8-inch square baking dish coated with cooking spray. Bake the chicken, uncovered, for 25 minutes.

Spoon the cranberry sauce over the stuffed chicken breasts. Top them with slices of Brie (if desired, remove the rind from the Brie). Bake the chicken, uncovered, for 10 to 15 minutes longer or until a thermometer inserted into the thickest part reads 165°. Discard the toothpicks before serving the chicken. If desired, garnish it with rosemary sprigs.

Let leftover cranberry Brie chicken cool slightly, then transfer it to an airtight container and refrigerate for up to four days. The breading will soften as it sits, especially under the cranberry sauce and melted Brie, but it’ll still be tasty once reheated.

Cranberry Brie chicken tastes best fresh out of the oven, but you can absolutely get a head start on prepping the recipe. Make the spinach filling, and stuff the chicken breasts, securing them with toothpicks. Cover and refrigerate both for up to 24 hours.

When you’re ready to make dinner, dip the chicken in the egg, coat it with bread crumbs and bake it as directed. Save the cranberry sauce and Brie for the last 10 to 15 minutes of baking. Waiting to coat the chicken until just before baking helps keep the bread crumbs from getting soggy.

Reheat cranberry Brie chicken, loosely covered with foil, in a 350° oven until it’s warmed through to 165°. The microwave also works for single servings, but the breading will be a little soggier.

We love Brie here because its mild flavor and creamy texture pair so well with the tart cranberry sauce, but it’s not your only option. Camembert has a similar creamy texture and earthy flavor, or you could use goat cheese if you want something bolder and tangier. For a milder, kid-friendly option, try mozzarella or fontina. Both melt beautifully into a gooey, cheesy topping.

Boneless skinless chicken thighs can work in this recipe, but their smaller size makes them a little trickier to pound thin and fold around the spinach filling. If possible, choose larger thighs, and use toothpicks to keep the filling tucked inside. Since thighs vary in size and thickness, you may need to adjust baking time. Use a meat thermometer to make sure the chicken reaches an internal temperature of 165° before serving it.

Cranberry Brie chicken fits right in with holiday favorites like creamy mashed potatoes, roasted Brussels sprouts, stuffing or green bean casserole. For a more casual weeknight dinner, serve it over hot, fluffy rice to soak up the extra cranberry sauce, or pair it with roasted sweet potatoes or a simple green salad. And you can’t go wrong with a side of crusty bread, warm buttermilk biscuits or cornbread!

#6588. $22 Fries at Marcel Are One of New York's Finest Little Luxuries

This is Highly Recommend, a column dedicated to what we’re eating, drinking, and buying.

I recently celebrated a dear friend's birthday at Marcel 945 Madison, the much buzzed about restaurant at Sotheby's global headquarters (RIP, old Whitney) on the Upper East Side of New York. Inside the Breuer Building, named for its Brutalist architect, it is a space to behold, equal parts concrete and midcentury walnut accents. Every detail—the luscious lighting, the forged flatware, the tufted mohair banquettes—is exquisitely considered and, likely, for sale.

In this beautiful room full of beautiful people, I could not take my eyes off the frites, priced at $22 under the "Accompagnements" section of the menu in Chroma sans serif type.

Skinny but not shoestring, long, golden, and perfectly salted, they practically glowed from within a napkin-lined bread basket. Every frite was pert, not a single one enervated under a mountain of hot fries. There was no oily outline at the bottom, either.

When I first saw the large portion, I felt a brief wave of doubt: Could we even finish these? How silly of me. We made quick work of the basket, with not a single spud left behind. These fries are so good, they do not need the crutch of a condiment—though they did reach another stratosphere when dipped in plain mayonnaise.

“I like them best with the chicken jus in the roasted chicken dish, or sauce au poivre with the filet de boeuf,” recommends Marie-Aude Rose, chef-partner at Marcel.

When people talk about life's little luxuries, they're talking about these frites. If the best McDonald's fries spent a transformative semester in Paris, they would be a little closer—but still untouchable—to Marcel's frites.

Is $22 pricy? Yes. But we're not talking about a paltry handful landing in a stainless steel cup lined with parchment. These are impeccable, best-in-class wonders, elegantly and generously presented.

I was so in awe that I had to know the deliberate thinking that must be responsible for such perfection. Rose says it is a long process. The kitchen begins with Idaho Russet, chosen not just for taste, but for length and sugar and moisture content that she calls “adequate to frying.”

The potatoes are cut with a French fry cutter, soaked in water, then dried and pre-fried in peanut oil at 160C (320F). During service, they are fried again in clean peanut oil at 180C (356F) and then seasoned with La Baleine fine sea salt, Rose’s salt of choice for seasoning all food at the restaurant.

"Time is important,” Rose said. “You cannot rush cooking.”

Please, chef, take all the time you need.

#6587. This Genius Trick Makes Perfectly Portioned Cinnamon Rolls—No Ruler or Guessing Required

This clever little move turns your knife into a measuring guide for cinnamon rolls.

I have no objection to a shortcut in the kitchen. I’m happy to let boxed cake mix handle dessert or a great jar of pasta sauce get dinner moving. But I just can’t make peace with cinnamon rolls from a can. I want to love them. I appreciate the convenience, and I understand the appeal of having warm cinnamon rolls before the coffee is finished brewing. They just never quite satisfy that craving for a warm, deliciously gooey cinnamon roll.

Some viral upgrades make a compelling case—particularly the heavy cream bath and generous additions of butter and brown sugar. But my long-standing love for cinnamon rolls has much more to do with the soft, pillowy dough, so I’m willing to wait through a rise or two.

Having committed to that, though, I’m still interested in anything that makes the process easier. So when I saw a video of someone flipping a knife over a log of cinnamon roll dough to mark perfectly even portions, I wanted to try it. Cutting equal slices by eye can involve a surprising amount of second-guessing when you’d really just like to get them in the pan. I made our classic cinnamon roll recipe and put the trick to the test.

The clever part of this trick is that the knife becomes its own measurement. Rather than judging the thickness of each slice, you use the width of the blade to mark equal portions along the dough roll before slicing it into pieces.

Once your dough is filled and rolled into a log, gently lay the blade flat across the top at one end, with the knife running crosswise over the log. Then flip it onto its opposite flat side, moving along the dough one blade-width at a time. It looks a little like the knife is doing small somersaults, with its edge leaving a light indentation at each turn.

Continue down the log, using just enough pressure to leave visible marks. Then go back and slice through the dough at those marks.

This worked beautifully with our classic cinnamon rolls, but the same technique would work with just about any cinnamon roll recipe. The turning motion was simple, and the knife left an evenly spaced cutting guide along the dough. Once the marks were there, I could slice the rolls without measuring each one or estimating where the next cut should go.

I particularly liked being able to see all the portions before I started cutting. It made the job feel settled: The spacing was already worked out, and all I had to do was follow it. For something that takes so little effort, it’s a useful bit of precision.

This is the kind of cinnamon roll shortcut I can get behind. I still get the homemade rolls I wanted, but there’s one less thing to fuss over before the pan goes into the oven.

#6586. Chrissy Teigen Reveals Her Go-To Date Night Food With John Legend—And It’s Surprisingly Simple

Chrissy Teigen and John Legend might be one of Hollywood's most recognizable couples, but apparently, even they struggle to find time for a date night.

On the latest episode of Déjà Food, the cookbook author opens up about her favorite meals with Legend, revealing that between their busy schedules and raising four children, finding time for a night out isn’t always easy. But when they do manage to sneak away, there’s one type of food they almost always gravitate toward.

“We don't often get date nights, but when we do, it's Italian,” Teigen says.

And considering the couple’s history, that actually makes perfect sense.

Italy has played a pretty significant role in their relationship. The two tied the knot in Lake Como in 2013 and returned to the same destination to celebrate their 10th wedding anniversary.

During the interview, Teigen recalls enjoying an Italian feast at their anniversary celebration and reveals that their wedding dinner featured pasta served from a large cheese wheel.

Italian food also seems to be the couple's preferred choice for birthdays. Teigen recalls celebrating one of her birthdays in Italy, where she believes she ate porcini mushroom risotto, which she describes as one of her favorite dishes.

And for Legend's birthday, she organized a dinner with his New York friends at Casa Cipriani.

“I surprised him with his New York friends, and we went to Casa Cipriani and had an incredible meal,” she says. “Everything they have there is incredible.”

Of course, not every date night has been quite so effortless.

Teigen also shares a story about one of the first times she splurged on dinner for Legend early in their relationship. After months of him treating her, she decided it was finally her turn to pick up the check at a restaurant from Chef Daniel Boulud.

But she was so nervous about her card potentially being declined that she brought a large amount of cash and spent the entire meal mentally calculating the bill.

Things got especially stressful when she ordered a margarita that cost approximately $42.

“I was so nervous, but I had enough cash,” she recalls, before admitting that she thinks Legend ended up paying the tip.

Thankfully, their restaurant dates seem to have become a little less stressful over the years.

And while the couple clearly appreciates an elaborate Italian dinner, Teigen also reveals that Legend recently made her a Kirkland Signature Costco Chicken Bake at home.

“It was like a Hot Pocket, but huge,” she says.

So apparently, the secret to keeping date night interesting is a little Italian food, an occasional fancy restaurant, and sometimes a really big Costco Chicken Bake.

A new program aims to help scientists figure out how the ingredients of the universe formed early galaxies, which lit up the cosmos after a "dark age."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists are getting a new glimpse of how the first galaxies came to be. In a stunning new simulation, researchers charted the aftermath of the universe's "dark age," including the appearance of the first galaxies that began to shine about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

Lumina, the program behind the simulation, catalogs 2 billion years of cosmic time and represents a decent chunk of the 13.8 billion-year-old history of our universe. The results were published Monday (Oct. 26) in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

"Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this," study co-author Mark Vogelsberger, a professor of physics at MIT, said in a statement. "The difference between the smallest and largest scales that we simulate is larger than in any other simulation."

A video published alongside the paper shows what the scientists saw. The team zoomed in on an area roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide to learn more about how the ingredients of space create galaxies.

This section of the Lumina simulation shows the gas temperature in different parts of the early universe, with redder areas showing active galaxy clusters.

In the earliest years of our universe, a fog of neutral hydrogen atoms gradually built up, blocking out the light of the first stars. The hydrogen served as a "shroud" and didn't make light visible until galaxies began to form. This ancient, enshrouded period is known as the Cosmic Dark Age.

The video begins in the middle of this epoch, at roughly 45 million years after the Big Bang. Zooming in on one small part of the simulated universe, it slowly reveals a gassy halo giving way to young galaxies shining brightly within it. Included in the calculations are dark matter, stars, gas and radiation — all contributing to the reemergence of cosmic light.

"We see this is where the first galaxies form," first author Oliver Zier, a former postdoctoral researcher and computational astrophysicist at MIT who is now at Harvard University, said in the statement. "And the first stars form in those first galaxies. Those stars then create radiation. The simulation then tracks that radiation, and we can zoom way out to see how that radiation travels out from stars, through the universe, until at some point it ionizes some neutral hydrogen."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Lumina aims to show off two phenomena key to the young universe's history: hydrogen reionization and helium reionization — a first for a program of its kind. Reionization describes how the intergalactic medium, or the area between galaxies, changed from neutral hydrogen to negatively charged ions.

Hydrogen reionization took place when ultraviolet light from young stars and galaxies hit the hydrogen, removing negatively charged electrons from the hydrogen molecules — a process that also allowed light to shine through the fog. Helium reionization happened when supermassive black holes, which have a lot of energy, broke apart neutral helium molecules.

The team said the simulation could eventually be used to validate telescope observations of the early universe, especially those focused on mapping many galaxies at the same time.

Zier, O., Smith, A., Shen, X., Liu, R., Kannan, R., Koehler, S. M., Springel, V., Pakmor, R., Vogelsberger, M., Bulichi, T., & Hernquist, L. (2026). Introducing the lumina project: large-volume radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of the epochs of hydrogen and helium reionization. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 552(4). https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stag1469
